items.title: Early labour at home
doThis: Keep her gently moving in the day and resting at night.
Bring drinks (isotonic ones help) and light snacks.
Run her a warm bath.
Paracetamol is safe in labour.
Rub her back and breathe slowly with her.
If it drags on, sleep in shifts so one of you is fresh later.
avoidThis: Heading in too early: she may be sent home.
Both of you staying up all night.

provenance.sourceTitle: NHS: The stages of labour and birth

items.title: Timing contractions
doThis: Time a handful to see the pattern, then stop.
Time again when things change.
Measure from the start of one to the start of the next.
Note how long each one lasts, from start to end.
Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together.
avoidThis: Staring at the timer instead of at her.
Waiting on the numbers if you're worried: call the unit any time.

provenance.sourceTitle: NHS: Signs that labour has begun

items.title: If she's being induced
doThis: Expect it to take a long time: often 24 to 48 hours.
Pack food, chargers and something to do.
Ask what each step is and what comes next.
Use BRAIN at each step: it's her choice throughout.
Expect contractions on the drip to be stronger.
avoidThis: Expecting a quick start.
Letting your own boredom show.

items.title: Positions that help
doThis: Help her stay upright and moving: standing, leaning forward, kneeling, all fours or a birth ball.
With an epidural, help her lie on her side rather than flat.
Prompt a trip to the loo every 2 to 3 hours: a full bladder can slow things down.
avoidThis: Letting her lie flat on her back.

provenance.sourceTitle: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals: Intrapartum care guideline v13

items.title: Back pain and back-to-back babies
doThis: Try forward-leaning and all-fours positions.
Press firmly on her lower back during contractions.
Try a double hip squeeze.
Use heat or ice on her back.
avoidThis: Promising a position will turn the baby: it eases the pain, but there's no good evidence it turns baby.

provenance.sourceTitle: NCT: Baby positions in the womb and birth

items.title: Hands-on comfort
doThis: Cool flannel on her face and neck.
Water spray or a fan.
Sips from a bottle with a straw.
Lip balm and a hair tie within reach.
Firm lower-back massage, if she wants it.
avoidThis: Taking it personally if she suddenly doesn't want to be touched.

provenance.sourceTitle: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals: Intrapartum care guideline v13

items.title: Breathe with her
doThis: Breathe slowly with her, with a long breath out.
Keep your voice low and steady.
Hold eye contact through the peak if she wants it.
Help her change position when she wants to.
avoidThis: Counting out loud unless she's asked you to.

provenance.sourceTitle: NHS: Tips for your birth partner

items.title: Guard the room
doThis: Dim the lights and put her music on.
Keep the chatter down.
Handle the phone and the family updates.
Keep away any visitors she doesn't want.
avoidThis: Inviting people in.
Texting the group chat in front of her.

provenance.sourceTitle: NCT: Ten tips for birth partners

items.title: What to say
doThis: "You're doing it."
"That one's gone."
"Every contraction brings the baby closer."
"I'm so proud of you."
Don't ask, do: hold the straw to her lips rather than asking if she wants a drink.
avoidThis: "I know how you feel."
Mentioning that you're tired or hungry.
A stream of questions.
Letting panic show.

provenance.sourceTitle: Pediatrix: How to support your partner in labor

items.title: Your job with pain relief
doThis: TENS: put it on early, before the pain is strong. Not in water.
Gas and air: hand her the mouthpiece as a contraction starts. It takes 15 to 20 seconds to work.
Pethidine or diamorphine: watch for sickness. No pool for 2 hours afterwards.
Remifentanil: remind her to press the button as each contraction starts, and tell staff if she's very drowsy.
Epidural: help her curl up and stay still while it goes in, and remind her to change sides every hour.
avoidThis: Using the gas and air yourself.
Watching the epidural needle if you're squeamish: look away, or step out if asked.

items.title: Speaking up for her
doThis: Use BRAIN: Benefits, Risks, Alternatives, Intuition, and what if we wait an hour?
Ask: "Is this an emergency or a recommendation?"
Ask: "Can we have five minutes to decide?"
Say: "She can't take this in right now, give us a minute."
If something feels wrong: tell the midwife, use the call bell, ask for the coordinator or a doctor's review.
In England, ask for a Martha's Rule call if she's getting worse and you're not being heard.
avoidThis: Agreeing to anything on her behalf: only she can consent.
Asking "Am I allowed?": staff need her permission, not the other way round.

items.title: Look after yourself
doThis: Eat and drink: bring your own snacks.
Sit down before you feel faint, and don't lock your knees.
Look away during the epidural or the incision if you need to.
Watch the midwife's face, not the floor: their calm tells you a lot.
Say "I'm scared, tell me what to do."
avoidThis: Eating strong-smelling food in the room.
Complaining that you're tired or hungry.
Popping home without asking the midwife how long you realistically have.

provenance.sourceTitle: NCT: Ten tips for birth partners

items.title: When she says she can't do it
doThis: Stay close and stay calm.
Use short, firm phrases and eye contact.
Tell her this intensity means she's close.
Offer sips of water and a cool cloth.
Call the midwife if she feels like pushing.
avoidThis: Taking swearing or shouting personally.
Leaving the room.

provenance.sourceTitle: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals: Intrapartum care guideline v13

items.title: Pushing
doThis: Stand by her head or shoulder, where she can see you.
Support her leg or back in the position she's chosen.
Echo what the midwife says, calmly.
When the midwife says pant, pant with her.
avoidThis: Counting loudly unless she's asked you to.
Taking photos or filming without her agreement beforehand.

provenance.sourceTitle: NHS: The stages of labour and birth

items.title: The first hour
doThis: Ask for baby straight onto her bare chest, before the cord is cut.
Keep skin-to-skin going for at least an hour, or until the first feed.
If she's on gas and air, drowsy, or in theatre under general anaesthetic, do skin-to-skin yourself.
Cut the cord after at least a minute, if you've agreed to.
Keep baby's face visible, and tell staff straight away if anything worries you.
avoidThis: Rushing the weighing and the photos: they can wait.

provenance.sourceTitle: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly: Skin-to-skin contact

items.title: If she goes to theatre
doThis: With a spinal, sit by her head behind the screen.
Baby is usually out in 5 to 10 minutes; the whole operation takes 40 to 50.
Ask about skin-to-skin in theatre.
Under general anaesthetic you'll be asked to wait nearby: ask where, and ask for baby for skin-to-skin in recovery.
avoidThis: Watching the incision if you're squeamish: watch her face instead.

items.title: Emergency caesarean (Category 1)
doThis: Expect it to be fast: birth within about 30 minutes of the decision.
Expect a lot of people and noise. That's the team working.
Go where you're asked to wait, and ask who will update you.
Ask for baby for skin-to-skin as soon as you can.
avoidThis: Reading being asked to leave as bad news: partners can't be in theatre under general anaesthetic.
